## Agentic video understanding  {% id="agentic-video-understanding" %}

By default, video inputs use static processing (extracting frames at 1 FPS) across all models, including Gemini 4.
Gemini 4 Carbon, Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, 3.8 Flash, 3.6 Flash, and 3.5 Flash Lite models also support
**agentic video understanding**, an opt-in mode where the model dynamically explores the video
timeline, selectively inspecting transcripts and adaptively adjusting frame
rates and resolution on the fly based on the prompt.

| **Mode** | **Description** | **Supported models** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Static** (default) | Extracts frames at a fixed rate (1 FPS) and places them into context in a single pass. Default for all Gemini models, including Gemini 4. | All Gemini models |
| **Agentic** | The model dynamically navigates the video timeline, loading only the content it needs based on the prompt. Up to 88% more token-efficient and ~7% higher quality on long-form content. | Gemini 4 Carbon, Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Hydrogen, 3.8 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash Lite |

### Choose a processing mode  {% id="when-to-use" %}

Select the processing mode that matches your video length and query type:

- **Static (default):** Best for short clips (under 5 minutes), broad full-video summaries where the entire recording is relevant, latency-sensitive queries, or frame-level precision across the entire clip. On short videos or broad prompts that require inspecting most of the video, static processing avoids the additional thinking tokens (`total_thought_tokens`) and tool-call round-trips (`total_tool_use_tokens`) incurred by timeline navigation.
- **Agentic:** Best for long-form videos (over 5–10 minutes), needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, or queries targeting specific moments or topics. The model inspects transcripts first and loads only relevant visual segments on demand, reducing video input token usage by up to 88% without filling the context window.

Agentic video processing can take longer on long videos because the model
performs multiple inspection passes to navigate the timeline. To avoid losing
progress if a network connection drops, the following example uses
the `background` parameter to run the task asynchronously on the server. You can also
run requests synchronously without background execution by omitting the `background`
parameter, which works well for shorter videos.

For details on polling, retrieving results, and managing background tasks, see
the [background execution](/docs/background-execution) guide.

    sleep 5
    interaction=$(curl -s "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions/$id" \

echo "$interaction" | jq '.'

### Multi-turn video conversations  {% id="multi-turn-video" %}

Video context is preserved across turns in a conversation. When using agentic
processing:

- **Stateful mode** (using `previous_interaction_id`): The server retains the
  video context. No additional handling is needed.
- **Stateless mode** (using `step_list`): In stateless mode, the response
  includes `processing_call` and `processing_result` steps that encode the
  video context. You must include all steps from the response in your next
  request's `step_list` to preserve video context. While omitting them does not
  currently return an API error, the video context is lost, significantly
  reducing response quality on follow-up questions. Note that returned steps
  sent in subsequent requests contribute to input token counts.

## Extract detailed insights from video  {% id="transcribe-video" %}

Gemini models offer powerful capabilities for understanding video content by
processing information from both the **audio and visual** streams. This lets you
extract a rich set of details, including generating descriptions of what is
happening in a video and answering questions about its content.

For visual descriptions, the model samples the video at a rate of **1 frame
per second** (FPS). This default sampling rate works well for most content, but
note that it may miss details in videos with rapid motion or quick scene
changes.

### Set clipping intervals  {% id="clipping-intervals" %}

You can clip video by setting `start_offset` and `end_offset` in the `processing` configuration object. Specify each offset as a string of seconds ending with `"s"`, such as `"1200s"` or `"10.5s"`.

## Supported video formats  {% id="supported-formats" %}

Gemini supports the following video format MIME types:

* `video/mp4`
* `video/mpeg`
* `video/mov`
* `video/avi`
* `video/x-flv`
* `video/mpg`
* `video/webm`
* `video/wmv`
* `video/3gpp`

## Technical details about videos  {% id="technical-details-video" %}

- **Supported models and context**: All Gemini models can process video data.  -   Models with a 1M context window can process videos up to 3 hours long by
    default (at low media resolution), or up to 1 hour long at high media
    resolution.

- **Processing modes**: Gemini 4 Carbon, Gemini 4 Argon, 3.8 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash Lite,
  and later models support two video processing modes:  -   **Static**: Frames are extracted at 1 FPS and placed into context (default
    for all models). Audio is processed at 1Kbps (single channel).
    Timestamps are added every second. Best for short clips or when every frame
    matters (such as frame-by-frame inspection). Note that fast action sequences
    might lose detail due to the 1 FPS sampling rate.
  -   **Agentic**: The model dynamically navigates the video, loading
    transcript and/or frames and/or audio on demand. This uses up to 88%

fewer tokens for long-form content, though navigation may increase Time to First Token (TTFT) and total token usage on short clips (<5 minutes) or broad queries due to
    internal reasoning and tool round-trips. Best
    for long-form videos and targeted queries to optimize token costs and response quality.
    Supported on Gemini 4 Carbon, Gemini 4 Argon, 3.8 Flash, 3.6 Flash, and 3.5 Flash Lite.
    See [Agentic video understanding](/docs/video-understanding#agentic-video-understanding) for details.

- **Token calculation (static mode)**: Each second of video is tokenized as
  follows:  -   Individual frames (sampled at 1 FPS):    -   If `media_resolution` is set to low, frames are tokenized at 66
      tokens per frame.
    -   Otherwise, frames are tokenized at 258 tokens per frame.

-   Audio: 32 tokens per second.
  -   Metadata is also included.
  -   Total: Approximately 100 tokens per second of video at default (low) media
    resolution, or approximately 300 tokens per second of video at high media
    resolution.

- **Token calculation (agentic mode)**: Token usage varies based on content
  complexity and the model's navigation strategy. Navigation reasoning tokens
  generated during video exploration are accounted as **thought tokens**
  (`total_thought_tokens`), while frames, audio, and transcript loaded on
  demand are accounted as tool use tokens (`total_tool_use_tokens`).
  Agentic processing typically uses up to 88% fewer total tokens than static
  processing for long-form content because the model loads only the transcript
  and/or frames and/or audio it needs to answer the prompt (see the
  [tokens guide](/docs/tokens#video)).
- **Media resolution**: Gemini 3 introduces granular control over multimodal
  vision processing with the `media_resolution` parameter. The

`media_resolution` parameter determines the **maximum number of tokens
  allocated per input image or video frame.** Higher resolutions improve the
  model's ability to read fine text or identify small details, but increase
  token usage and latency. The `media_resolution` and `processing` parameters
  are independent: you can set both on the same video input.

For more details on token calculations, see the
[tokens](/docs/tokens) guide.

- **Timestamp format**: When referring to specific moments in a video within
  your prompt, use the `MM:SS` format (e.g., `01:15` for 1 minute and 15
  seconds).
- **Prompt placement**: If combining text and a single video, place the text prompt
  *after* the video part in the `input` array.
- **Timeouts for long requests**: For videos that require extended
  processing time or complex multi-step reasoning, use streaming or
  [background execution](/docs/background-execution).
  Synchronous, non-streaming requests that experience backend retries under
  high demand can exceed connection or authentication token validity windows,
  which may surface as unexpected `401 Unauthorized` or timeout errors.
  Streaming keeps the connection active and surfaces intermediate reasoning

and tool call progress.

# Document understanding

Gemini models can process documents in PDF format, using native
vision to understand entire document contexts. This goes beyond
just text extraction, allowing Gemini to:

*   Analyze and interpret content, including text, images, diagrams,
  charts, and tables, even in long documents up to 1000 pages.

*   Extract information into [structured output](/docs/structured-output) formats.

*   Summarize and answer questions based on both the visual and textual elements
  in a document.

*   Transcribe document content (e.g. to HTML), preserving layouts and
  formatting, for use in downstream applications.

You can also pass Microsoft Office and OpenDocument files, such as Word
documents, PowerPoint presentations, and Excel spreadsheets. For details, see
[Office and OpenDocument files](/docs/document-processing#office-documents).
Other non-PDF documents, such as TXT, Markdown, or HTML files, are processed as
plain text, which eliminates context like charts or formatting.

You can pass PDF data inline in the request. This is best
suited for smaller documents or temporary processing where you don't need to
reference the file in subsequent requests. We recommend using the
[Files API](/docs/document-processing#large-pdfs)
for larger documents that you need to refer to in multi-turn interactions to
improve request latency and reduce bandwidth usage.

## Office and OpenDocument files  {% id="office-documents" %}

Gemini models can process Microsoft Office and OpenDocument files. Pass them
the same way as PDFs, either inline or with the Files API, using a `document`
content block and one of the following MIME types:

| File type | Extension | MIME type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Documents | `.docx` | `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document` |
|  | `.doc` | `application/msword` |
|  | `.dotx` | `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.template` |
|  | `.odt` | `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.text` |
| Presentations | `.pptx` | `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation` |
|  | `.ppt` | `application/vnd.ms-powerpoint` |
|  | `.odp` | `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.presentation` |
| Spreadsheets | `.xlsx` | `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet` |
|  | `.xls` | `application/vnd.ms-excel` |
|  | `.ods` | `application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.spreadsheet` |

These files are processed as follows:

* **DOCX, DOTX, ODT, and PPTX files**: The model receives the text of the
  whole file, plus embedded images for DOCX and PPTX files. Pages and slides
  aren't rendered as images, so page layout and visual elements such as
  charts might not be preserved.
* **DOC, PPT, and ODP files**: Each page or slide is rendered as an image,
  so the model can interpret layouts, charts, and images. The whole file is
  processed.
* **XLSX and XLS files**: Only the **first sheet** is read. Its contents are
  converted to CSV, so the model receives the cell values but not formulas or
  formatting.
* **ODS files**: Only the **first sheet** is read. The model receives its cell
  data and formulas.

Other sheets in a workbook are ignored. To analyze a different sheet, move it to
the first position or save it as a separate file.

Files are processed the same way whether you pass them in a request or a tool
returns them in a [function response](/docs/function-calling#multimodal).
The existing file size and page limits apply to the whole file.

The following example uploads a PowerPoint presentation with the Files API and
asks the model to summarize it:

{% tabs %}
  {% tab filename="sample.py" label="Python" %}
  ```python
  from google import genai

client = genai.Client()

deck = client.files.upload(
      file="quarterly_review.pptx",
      config={
          "mime_type": "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.presentationml.presentation"
      },
  )

## Technical details  {% id="technical-details" %}

Gemini supports PDF files up to 50MB or 1000 pages. This limit applies
to both inline data and Files API uploads. Each document page is equivalent to
258 tokens.

While there are no specific limits to the number of pixels in a document besides
the model's [context window](/docs/long-context), larger pages are
scaled down to a maximum resolution of 3072 x 3072 while preserving their
original aspect ratio, while smaller pages are scaled up to 768 x 768 pixels.
There is no cost reduction for pages at lower sizes, other than bandwidth, or
performance improvement for pages at higher resolution.

### Gemini 3 models  {% id="gemini-3-models" %}

Gemini 3 introduces granular control over multimodal vision processing with the
`media_resolution` parameter. You can now set the resolution to low, medium, or
high per individual media part. With this addition, the processing of PDF
documents has been updated:

1.   **Native text inclusion:** Text natively embedded in the PDF is extracted
  and provided to the model.

2.   **Billing & token reporting:**

*     You are **not charged** for tokens originating from the extracted
    **native text** in PDFs.

*     In the `usage_metadata` section of the API response, tokens generated
    from processing PDF pages (as images) are now counted under the `IMAGE`
    modality, not a separate `DOCUMENT` modality as in some earlier
    versions.

For more details about the media resolution parameter, see the
[Media resolution](/docs/media-resolution) guide.

### Document types  {% id="document-types" %}

Document vision meaningfully understands PDFs and DOC, PPT, and ODP files,
which are rendered as page images. DOCX, DOTX, ODT, and PPTX files are converted
to text, and spreadsheets are read as tabular data. For details, see
[Office and OpenDocument files](/docs/document-processing#office-documents).

Technically, you can pass other MIME types for document understanding, like
TXT, Markdown, HTML, XML, etc. However, these types are extracted as pure
text, which means the model can't understand the visual elements present in a
rendered file. Any file-type specifics like charts, diagrams, HTML tags,
Markdown formatting, etc., will be lost.

To learn about other file input methods, see the
[File input methods](/docs/file-input-methods) guide.

### Best practices  {% id="best-practices" %}

For best results:

* Rotate pages to the correct orientation before uploading.
* Avoid blurry pages.
* If using a single page, place the text prompt after the page.

## Overview  {% id="overview" %}

Gemini can analyze and understand audio input and generate text responses,
enabling use cases like:

* Describe, summarize, or answer questions about audio content
* Transcription and translation (speech to text)
* Speaker diarization (identifying different speakers)
* Emotion detection in speech and music
* Analyzing specific segments with timestamps

For real-time voice and video interactions, see the
[Live API](/docs/live-api).
For dedicated speech to text models with support for real-time transcription,
use the [Google Cloud Speech-to-Text API](https://cloud.google.com/speech-to-text).

For the complete list of supported MIME types and parameter schemas, see the [Interactions API reference](/api-reference/interactions-api#Resource:Content).

## Technical details about audio  {% id="technical-details" %}

* **Tokens**: 32 tokens per second of audio (1 minute = 1,920 tokens)
* **Non-speech**: Gemini understands non-speech sounds (birdsong, sirens, etc.)
* **Max length**: 9.5 hours of audio per prompt
* **Resolution**: Downsampled to 16 Kbps
* **Channels**: Multi-channel audio combined to single channel

# Gemini thinking

[Gemini models](/docs/models) use a
"thinking process" that significantly improves their reasoning and multi-step
planning abilities, making them highly effective for complex tasks such as
coding, advanced mathematics, and data analysis.

When you use a thinking model, Gemini reasons internally before responding. The
Interactions API surfaces this reasoning via `thought` steps, dedicated steps
that appear chronologically alongside function calls, user inputs or model
outputs in the `steps` array.

Every thought step contains two fields:

{% table %}
  * Field
  * Required
  * Description

---

* `signature`
  * ✅ Yes
  * An encrypted representation of the model's internal reasoning state. Always present, even when the model performs minimal reasoning.

---

* `summary`
  * ❌ No
  * An array of content (text and/or images) summarizing the reasoning. May be empty depending on the [`thinking_summaries`](/api-reference/interactions-api) config, whether the model performed enough reasoning, or the content type (for example, image latents may not have text summaries).
{% /table %}

{% callout type="note" %}
  The Interactions API handles thoughts and signatures differently than the
  `generateContent` API:

- In the `generateContent` API, there are no dedicated thought blocks. Because
    of this, signatures are metadata that can be attached to any part, such as
    living inside `functionCall` parts or the final part of a response.
  - In the Interactions API, thoughts are a first-class representation as
    dedicated `thought` steps. Because of this signatures are limited exclusively
    to two known locations, `thought` steps, or built-in tool steps (like
    `google_search_call`/ `google_search_result`). They never appear on user
    inputs, model outputs, or standard function calls.

{% /callout %}

Your code should always handle thought blocks where `summary` is empty or
absent.

## Streaming with thinking  {% id="streaming-with-thinking" %}

Use streaming to receive incremental thought summaries during generation.
Thought blocks are delivered using Server-Sent Events (SSE) with two distinct
delta types:

| Delta type | Contains | When sent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `thought_summary` | Text or image summary content | One or more deltas with incremental summary |
| `thought_signature` | The cryptographic signature | the last delta before `step.stop` |

  Which house does each person live in?
  """

thoughts = ""

## Controlling thinking  {% id="thinking-levels" %}

Gemini models engage in dynamic thinking by default, automatically adjusting
the amount of reasoning effort based on the complexity of the request. You can
control this behavior using the `thinking_level` parameter.

| Model | Default Thinking | Levels Supported |
| --- | --- | --- |
| gemini-4-carbon | On (medium) | low, medium, high |
| gemini-4-argon | On (medium) | low, medium, high |
| gemini-4-hydrogen | On (high) | low, medium, high, xhigh |
| gemini-3.8-flash | On (medium) | low, medium, high |
| gemini-3.6-flash | On (medium) | minimal, low, medium, high |
| gemini-3.5-flash-lite | On (minimal) | minimal, low, medium, high |
| gemini-3.1-pro-preview | On (high) | low, medium, high |
| gemini-3.1-flash-lite | On (minimal) | minimal, low, medium, high |
| gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image | On (minimal) | minimal, high |
| gemini-3-flash-preview | On (high) | minimal, low, medium, high |
| gemini-3-pro-preview | On (high) | low, high |
| gemini-2.5-pro | On | low, medium, high |

| gemini-2.5-flash | On | low, medium, high |
| gemini-2.5-flash-lite | Off | low, medium, high |
| gemini-robotics-er-2-preview | On (high) | minimal, low, medium, high |

### Understanding thinking levels  {% id="understanding-thinking-levels" %}

The `thinking_level` is your main control over quality, latency, and token use in [Gemini 4 Hydrogen](/docs/whats-new-gemini-4-hydrogen). The model defaults to `high` and introduces `xhigh`:

| Thinking level | Token use | When to use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `low` | Fewest tokens, lowest latency | Cost- and latency-sensitive workloads, such as fast chat and high-throughput processing. Still capable on agentic tasks. |
| `medium` | Lower token use, faster responses | Interactive coding, live UI prototyping, responsive chat, and latency-sensitive tool calls. (Default on `gemini-4-carbon`, `gemini-4-argon`, `gemini-3.8-flash`, and `gemini-3.6-flash`.) |
| `high` (default on `gemini-4-hydrogen`) | Balanced intelligence and speed | Recommended default on `gemini-4-hydrogen` for most tasks, including complex coding, agentic execution, tool calling, and multimodal knowledge work. Maximum reasoning depth on `gemini-4-carbon`, `gemini-4-argon`, and Gemini 3 models. |

| `xhigh` | Most tokens, deepest reasoning | Reserve for hard, multi-step coding and agentic problems where `high` falls short, when you can trade higher latency and token use (supported on `gemini-4-hydrogen`). |
| `minimal` | Near-off thinking, lowest latency | Matches a near-off setting for most queries on `gemini-3.6-flash`, `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` (default), `gemini-3.1-flash-lite`, `gemini-3-flash-preview`, and `gemini-robotics-er-2-preview`. Not supported on Gemini 4 models or `gemini-3.8-flash`. |

### Token limits and `max_output_tokens` {% id="token-limits" %}

The
[`max_output_tokens`](/api-reference/interactions-api/create-interaction#request-body)
generation parameter sets the maximum number of tokens a response can generate,
including thought tokens.

When set, this parameter acts as a hard cutoff enforced by the infrastructure
without changing how the model allocates its thinking budget
(`thinking_level`).

If the model hits this limit while reasoning, it stops generating with status
`"incomplete"` and returns truncated or empty output (while still billing for
any thinking tokens generated). To reduce cost or latency without truncating
responses, lower `thinking_level` (`low` or `medium`) instead of setting a
small `max_output_tokens`.

For Gemini 4 models (`gemini-4-carbon`, `gemini-4-argon`, and `gemini-4-hydrogen`), keep the following context and output limits in mind:

* **Shared 1M context window:** Input, thinking, and output tokens share a single 1M-token context window (`1,048,576` tokens). If your input tokens plus `max_output_tokens` exceed 1,048,576 tokens, the API automatically caps the output limit to the remaining space in the context window (`1,048,576` minus your input tokens).
* **Default synchronous output cap (64K):** When `background=False`, the default `max_output_tokens` cap is 65,536 tokens. A single foreground hop generates up to 65,536 tokens for streaming calls and `gemini-4-hydrogen` non-streaming calls, or up to 32,768 tokens for non-streaming calls on `gemini-4-carbon` and `gemini-4-argon`.

* **Long decode (up to 1M tokens):** To allow Gemini 4 to reason and generate beyond `65,536` tokens (up to `1,048,576` tokens), configure `max_output_tokens` greater than `65,536` with `background=True` or client-side continuation. See [Long decode](/docs/long-decode) for details.

## Thought signatures  {% id="signatures" %}

Thought signatures are encrypted representations of the model's internal
reasoning. They are required to maintain reasoning continuity across multi-turn
interactions.

The Interactions API makes handling thought signatures much simpler than the
`generateContent` API.

### Stateful mode (Recommended)  {% id="stateful-mode-recommended" %}

By default, when you use the Interactions API in stateful mode (by setting
`store: true` and passing the `previous_interaction_id` in subsequent turns),
the server automatically manages the conversation state, including all thought
blocks and signatures. In this mode, you do not need to do anything regarding
signatures. They are handled entirely on the server side.

### Stateless mode  {% id="stateless-mode" %}

If you are managing the conversation state yourself (stateless mode) and passing
the full history of inputs and outputs in each request:

* You **MUST** always resend all `thought` blocks exactly as they were received from the model.
* You should **NOT** remove or modify thought blocks from the history, as they contain the signatures required for the model to continue its reasoning.
* When switching models within a session, you should still resend the previous model's thought blocks. The backend manages compatibility.

- **Review reasoning**: Analyze thought summaries to understand failures and improve prompts.
- **Control thinking budget**: Prompt the model to think less for lengthy outputs to save tokens.
- **Simple tasks**: Use minimal thinking for fact retrieval or classification (e.g., "Where was DeepMind founded?").
- **Moderate tasks**: Use default thinking for comparing concepts or creative reasoning (e.g., Compare electric and hybrid cars).
- **Complex tasks**: Use maximum thinking for advanced coding, math, or multi-step planning (e.g., Solve AIME math problems).

# Structured outputs

You can configure Gemini models to generate responses that adhere to a provided
JSON Schema. This ensures predictable, type-safe results and simplifies
extracting structured data from unstructured text.

Using structured outputs is ideal for:

* **Data extraction:** Pull specific information like names and dates from text.
* **Structured classification:** Classify text into predefined categories.
* **Agentic workflows:** Generate structured inputs for tools or APIs.

In addition to supporting JSON Schema in the REST API, the Google GenAI SDKs
allow defining schemas using
[Pydantic](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/) (Python) and
[Zod](https://zod.dev/) (JavaScript).

{% callout type="note" %}
  If you need yes/no probabilities, single-select choices, or rubric scores with
  calibrated confidence and zero output tokens, use the
  [Gemini Decision 1](/docs/models/gemini-decision-1) model with the
  [Decisions API](/docs/decisions-api).

This example showcases `anyOf` for conditional schemas and `enum` for

  from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

      summary: str = Field(description="A brief summary of the content.")
      is_safe: bool = Field(description="Whether the content is safe for all audiences.")

class ModerationResult(BaseModel):
      decision: Union[SpamDetails, NotSpamDetails]

* **`string`**: For text.
* **`number`**: For floating-point numbers.
* **`integer`**: For whole numbers.
* **`boolean`**: For true or false values.
* **`object`**: For structured data with key-value pairs.
* **`array`**: For lists of items.
* **`null`**: To allow a property to be null, include `"null"` in the type array
  (e.g., `{"type": ["string", "null"]}`).

These descriptive properties help guide the model:

* **`title`**: A short description of a property.
* **`description`**: A longer and more detailed description of a property.

### Type-specific properties  {% id="type-specific-properties" %}

**For `object` values:**

* **`properties`**: An object where each key is a property name and each value
  is a schema for that property.
* **`required`**: An array of strings, listing which properties are mandatory.
* **`additionalProperties`**: Controls whether properties not listed in
  `properties` are allowed. Can be a boolean or a schema.
* **Unsupported counting constraints**: `minProperties` and `maxProperties` are
  not enforced during constrained decoding and are ignored by the server.
  Validate property counts in your application code if needed.

**For `string` values:**

* **`enum`**: Lists a specific set of possible strings for classification tasks.
* **`format`**: Specifies a syntax for the string, such as `date-time`, `date`,
  `time`.
* **Unsupported length constraints**: `minLength` and `maxLength` are not
  enforced during constrained decoding and are ignored by the server.
  Validate string lengths in your application code if needed.

**For `number` and `integer` values:**

* **`enum`**: Lists a specific set of possible numeric values.
* **`minimum`**: The minimum inclusive value.
* **`maximum`**: The maximum inclusive value.

**For `array` values:**

* **`items`**: Defines the schema for all items in the array.
* **`prefixItems`**: Defines a list of schemas for the first N items, allowing
  for tuple-like structures.
* **`minItems`**: The minimum number of items in the array.
* **`maxItems`**: The maximum number of items in the array.
* **Unsupported array constraints**: `uniqueItems`, `contains`, `minContains`,
  and `maxContains` are not enforced during constrained decoding and are ignored
  by the server. Deduplicate items or check array contents in your application
  code if needed.

## Structured outputs versus function calling  {% id="vs-function-calling" %}

| Feature | Primary Use Case |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Structured Outputs** | **Formatting the final response.** Use when you want the model's *answer* in a specific format. |
| **Function Calling** | **Taking action during conversation.** Use when the model needs to *ask you* to perform a task before providing a final answer. |

## Best practices  {% id="best-practices" %}

* **Clear descriptions:** Use the `description` field to guide the model.
* **Strong typing:** Use specific types (`integer`, `string`, `enum`).
* **Prompt engineering:** Clearly state what you want the model to do.
* **Validation:** While output is syntactically correct JSON, always validate
  values in your application.
* **Error handling:** Implement robust error handling for schema-compliant but
  semantically incorrect outputs.

## Limitations  {% id="limitations" %}

* **Schema subset:** Not all JSON Schema features are supported.
* **Schema complexity:** Very large or deeply nested schemas may be rejected.
* **Unenforced constraints:** `minLength`, `maxLength`, `minProperties`,
  `maxProperties`, `uniqueItems`, `contains`, `minContains`, and `maxContains`
  (and their snake_case variants) are not enforced by the constrained decoding
  grammar engine. If these keywords are present in your schema (for instance,
  emitted automatically by Pydantic's `Field(min_length=...)` or Zod's
  `.min()`), the API automatically strips and ignores them during request
  normalization rather than returning an error. `minItems` and `maxItems` are
  enforced. To enforce the other constraints, validate the output in your client

application (e.g., using Pydantic `model_validate_json()` or Zod `.parse()`).

### Simplifying complex schemas  {% id="simplifying-complex-schemas" %}

When you request structured output, the API compiles your JSON Schema into a
state machine that constrains token generation. This state machine enforces
limits on total states, branching paths, and nesting depth. If your schema
exceeds these limits, the API rejects the request with a
`400 INVALID_ARGUMENT` error.

To fix schema rejection errors, reduce the structural depth and branching
factor of your schema. You can simplify complex schemas in several ways:

* **Move non-structural rules to descriptions:** Field `description` properties
  and system instructions guide the model without adding states to the output
  grammar. If complex constraints push your schema over the limit, move those
  rules into concise descriptions and validate the response in your application
  code.
* **Flatten nested objects and bound recursion:** Replace deeply nested object
  hierarchies with flatter structures. If you use `$defs` and `$ref` for
  recursive types, make the recursive reference optional or nullable. Avoid
  recursing through required properties or arrays with `minItems` greater than
  zero.
* **Reduce branching from optional fields, enums, and unions:** Optional
  properties, `enum` values, and `anyOf` branches multiply the branching paths

in the output grammar. Mark properties as `required` where possible and allow
  `null` values when a field can be empty. Trim large `enum` lists and simplify
  `anyOf` unions, or include the constraint in your prompt (for example, with a
  Pydantic schema) as a softer restriction.
* **Shorten property names and drop array or numeric bounds:** Property keys
  consume states proportional to their character length. Array bounds such as
  `minItems` and `maxItems` duplicate the item schema for each counted
  position, and numeric bounds (`minimum` and `maximum`) also increase the
  state space. Use concise property names, remove unused fields, and either
  include bounds in your prompt (for example, with a Pydantic schema) as a
  softer restriction or validate bounds in your application code.

# Function calling with the Gemini API

Function calling lets you connect models to external tools and APIs.
Instead of generating text responses, the model determines when to call specific
functions and provides the necessary parameters to execute real-world actions.
This allows the model to act as a bridge between natural language and real-world
actions and data. Function calling has 3 primary use cases:

- [**Take Actions:**](/docs/function-calling#meeting) Interact with external systems using APIs, such as
  scheduling appointments, creating invoices, sending emails, or controlling
  smart home devices.

### Stateless function calling  {% id="stateless-function-calling" %}

You can also use function calling in stateless mode by managing the conversation history on the client side and setting `store=false`.

In stateless mode, you must pass the full history of the conversation in the `input` field of each subsequent request. This history must include:

1. The initial `user_input` step.
2. All model-generated steps returned in Turn 1 (including `thought` and `function_call` steps) exactly as received.
3. The `function_result` step containing the output of your executed function.

    --arg fc_name "$FC_NAME" \
    --arg fc_id "$FC_ID" \

## Function declarations  {% id="function-declarations" %}

A function declaration is passed as a tool and includes:

* `type` (string): Must be `"function"` for custom functions.
* `name` (string): Unique function name (use underscores or camelCase).
* `description` (string): Clear explanation of the function's purpose.
* `parameters` (object): Input parameters the function expects.  *   `type` (string): Overall data type, such as `object`.
  *   `properties` (object): Individual parameters with type and description.
  *   `required` (array): Mandatory parameter names.

## Multimodal function responses  {% id="multimodal" %}

For Gemini 3 series models, you can include multimodal content in
the function response parts that you send to the model. The model can process
this multimodal content in its next turn to produce a more informed response.

To include multimodal data in a function response, include it as one or more content blocks in the `result` field of the `function_result` step. Each content block must specify its `type`. The following types are supported:

* **`text`**
* **`image`**: `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, `image/webp`
* **`document`**: `application/pdf`, `text/csv`, and
  [Office and OpenDocument files](/docs/document-processing#office-documents)
  (DOCX, DOC, DOTX, ODT, PPTX, PPT, ODP, XLSX, XLS, ODS)
* **`audio`**: [Supported audio formats](/docs/audio#supported-formats)
* **`video`**: [Supported video formats](/docs/video-understanding#supported-formats)
  (available in `v1beta` and `v1alpha`)

Each media block accepts either base64-encoded `data` or a `uri`, such as a
[Files API](/docs/files) URI. Files in function results are processed the same
way as the same file in a regular input. See
[Return files by URI](/docs/function-calling#file-uri) for an example.

If a block uses an unsupported MIME type, the API returns a `400
INVALID_ARGUMENT` error that names the field and lists the accepted types.

The following example shows how to send a function response containing image data back to the model in an interaction:

## Remote MCP (Model Context Protocol)  {% id="mcp" %}

Interactions API supports connecting to remote MCP servers to give the model access to external tools and services. You provide the server `name` and `url` in the tools configuration.

When using Remote MCP, be aware of the following constraints:

* **Server types**: Remote MCP only works with Streamable HTTP servers. SSE (Server-Sent Events) servers are not supported.
* **Naming**: MCP server names should not include the `-` character. Use `snake_case` server names instead.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `type` | `string` | Yes | Must be `"mcp_server"`. |
| `name` | `string` | No | A display name for the MCP server. |
| `url` | `string` | No | The full URL for the MCP server endpoint. |
| `headers` | `object` | No | Key-value pairs sent as HTTP headers with every request to the server (for example, authentication tokens). |
| `allowed_tools` | `array` | No | Restrict which tools from the server the agent may call. |

* **Function and Parameter Descriptions:** Be clear and specific.
* **Naming:** Use descriptive names without spaces or special characters.
* **Strong Typing:** Use specific types (integer, string, enum).
* **Tool Selection:** Keep active set to 10-20 tools maximum.
* **Prompt Engineering:** Provide context and instructions.
* **Validation:** Validate function calls before executing.
* **Error Handling:** Implement robust error handling.
* **Security:** Use appropriate authentication for external APIs.

## Workarounds for pre-tool text requirements  {% id="workarounds-for-pre-tool-text-requirements" %}

**Issue:** If your prompt requires the model to output structured text (XML, YAML, JSON, etc.) (e.g., `<UPDATE>...</UPDATE>`) immediately before making a tool call, the tool call may occasionally fail with `Malformed_Function_Call`.

**Solutions:** The following workarounds resolve this issue:

* **PREFERRED:** Instruct the model to put its pre-tool notes inside a dedicated `update()` function call instead of raw text (details below).
* Instruct the model to write notes as Markdown headers (`# UPDATE`, `## PLAN`) instead of structured text.
* Do not require the model to output text before tool calls.

### Preferred workaround: Wrap working notes in a dedicated function call  {% id="preferred-workaround" %}

Instead of the original instruction:

```html
Before calling a tool, in every response you MUST first output a single `<UPDATE>` part as specified, don't skip this part or any of required sub-tags within `<UPDATE>`.
```

Use this updated instruction:

```html
Before calling any other tool, in every response you MUST first call `update` with all required parameters (previous_step, plan, next_step, external).
```

And update all references to the old `<UPDATE>` XML format in the customer request. Then add the corresponding function declaration for the update function:

### Simplifying complex function schemas  {% id="simplifying-complex-schemas" %}

When you use `any` mode or define complex parameter schemas, the API compiles
your function declarations into a state machine that constrains token
generation. This state machine enforces limits on total states, branching
paths, and nesting depth. If the combined complexity of your tools exceeds
these limits, the API rejects the request with a `400 INVALID_ARGUMENT` error.

To fix schema rejection errors, reduce the structural depth and branching
factor of your declarations. You can simplify complex function schemas in
several ways:

* **Split large tool sets and move rules to descriptions:** Constrained
  decoding evaluates all declared tools together. Limit the number of functions
  in a single request and split monolithic functions into smaller, focused
  tools. Move complex formatting rules into field `description` properties or
  system instructions, which guide the model without expanding the grammar.
* **Flatten nested objects and bound recursion:** Replace deeply nested object
  hierarchies with flatter structures. If you use `$defs` and `$ref` for
  recursive types, make the recursive reference optional or nullable. Avoid
  recursing through required properties or arrays with `minItems` greater than
  zero.
* **Reduce branching from optional fields, enums, and unions:** Optional

properties, `enum` values, and `anyOf` branches multiply the branching paths
  in the output grammar. Mark properties as `required` where possible and allow
  `null` values when a field can be empty. Trim large `enum` lists and simplify
  `anyOf` unions, or include the constraint in your prompt (for example, with a
  Pydantic schema) as a softer restriction.
* **Shorten property names and drop array bounds:** Property keys consume
  states proportional to their character length. Array bounds such as
  `minItems` and `maxItems` also duplicate the item schema for each counted
  position. Use concise property names, remove unused fields, and either
  include array bounds in your prompt (for example, with a Pydantic schema) as
a softer restriction or check array lengths in your application code.

# Long context

Many Gemini models come with large context windows of 1 million or more tokens.
Historically, large language models (LLMs) were significantly limited by
the amount of text (or tokens) that could be passed to the model at one time.
The Gemini long context window unlocks many new use cases and developer
paradigms.

The code you already use for cases like [text
generation](/docs/text-generation) or [multimodal
inputs](/docs/image-understanding) will work without any changes with long
context.

This document gives you an overview of what you can achieve using models with
context windows of 1M and more tokens. The page gives a brief overview of
a context window, and explores how developers should think about long context,
various real world use cases for long context, and ways to optimize the usage
of long context.

For the context window sizes of specific models, see the
[Models](/docs/models) page.

## What is a context window?  {% id="what-is-context-window" %}

The basic way you use the Gemini models is by passing information (context)
to the model, which will subsequently generate a response. An analogy for the
context window is short term memory. There is a limited amount of information
that can be stored in someone's short term memory, and the same is true for
generative models.

In Gemini 4 (`gemini-4-carbon`, `gemini-4-argon`, and `gemini-4-hydrogen`), the 1M-token context window is **shared across input, thinking, and output tokens**, and the model can generate up to 1M output tokens using [long decode](/docs/long-decode). If your input tokens plus `max_output_tokens` exceed 1,048,576 tokens, the API automatically caps the output limit to the remaining space in the context window (`1,048,576` minus your input tokens). Earlier Gemini 3 and 2.5 models use separate 1M input and 64K output budgets.

You can read more about how models work in our [generative models
guide](/docs/prompting-strategies).

## Getting started with long context  {% id="getting-started-with-long-context" %}

Earlier versions of generative models were only able to process 8,000
tokens at a time. Newer models pushed this further by accepting 32,000 or even
128,000 tokens. Gemini is the first model capable of accepting 1 million tokens.

In practice, 1 million tokens would look like:

- 50,000 lines of code (with the standard 80 characters per line)
- All the text messages you have sent in the last 5 years
- 8 average length English novels
- Transcripts of over 200 average length podcast episodes

The more limited context windows common in many other models often require
strategies like arbitrarily dropping old messages, summarizing content, using
RAG with vector databases, or filtering prompts to save tokens.

While these techniques remain valuable in specific scenarios, Gemini's extensive
context window invites a more direct approach: providing all relevant
information upfront. Because Gemini models were purpose-built with massive
context capabilities, they demonstrate powerful in-context learning. For
example, using only in-context instructional materials (a 500-page reference
grammar, a dictionary, and ≈400 parallel sentences), Gemini
[learned to translate](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemini/gemini_v1_5_report.pdf)
from English to Kalamang—a Papuan language with
fewer than 200 speakers—with quality similar to a human learner using the same
materials. This illustrates the paradigm shift enabled by Gemini's long context,

empowering new possibilities through robust in-context learning.

## Long context use cases  {% id="long-context-use-cases" %}

While the standard use case for most generative models is still text input, the
Gemini model family enables a new paradigm of multimodal use cases. These
models can natively understand text, video, audio, and images. They are
accompanied by the [Gemini API that takes in multimodal file
types](/docs/files#prompt-guide) for
convenience.

### Long form text  {% id="long-form-text" %}

Text has proved to be the layer of intelligence underpinning much of the
momentum around LLMs. As mentioned earlier, much of the practical limitation of
LLMs was because of not having a large enough context window to do certain
tasks. This led to the rapid adoption of retrieval augmented generation (RAG)
and other techniques which dynamically provide the model with relevant
contextual information. Now, with larger and larger context windows, there are
new techniques becoming available which unlock new use cases.

Some emerging and standard use cases for text based long context include:

-   Summarizing large corpuses of text

-   Previous summarization options with smaller context models would require
    a sliding window or another technique to keep state of previous sections
    as new tokens are passed to the model

-   Question and answering

-   Historically this was only possible with RAG given the limited amount of
    context and models' factual recall being low

-   Agentic workflows

-   Text is the underpinning of how agents keep state of what they have done
    and what they need to do; not having enough information about the world
    and the agent's goal is a limitation on the reliability of agents

[Many-shot in-context learning](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.11018) is one of the
most unique capabilities unlocked by long context models. Research has shown
that taking the common "single shot" or "multi-shot" example paradigm, where the
model is presented with one or a few examples of a task, and scaling that up to
hundreds, thousands, or even hundreds of thousands of examples, can lead to
novel model capabilities. This many-shot approach has also been shown to perform
similarly to models which were fine-tuned for a specific task. For use cases
where a Gemini model's performance is not yet sufficient for a production
rollout, you can try the many-shot approach. As you might explore later in the
long context optimization section, context caching makes this type of high input

token workload much more economically feasible and even lower latency in some
cases.

### Long form video  {% id="long-form-video" %}

Video content's utility has long been constrained by the lack of accessibility
of the medium itself. It was hard to skim the content, transcripts often failed
to capture the nuance of a video, and most tools don't process image, text, and
audio together. With Gemini, the long-context text capabilities translate to
the ability to reason and answer questions about multimodal inputs with
sustained performance.

Some emerging and standard use cases for video long context include:

-   Video question and answering

-   Video memory, as shown with [Google's Project Astra](https://deepmind.google/technologies/gemini/project-astra/)

-   Video captioning

-   Video recommendation systems, by enriching existing metadata with new
  multimodal understanding

-   Video customization, by looking at a corpus of data and associated video
  metadata and then removing parts of videos that are not relevant to the
  viewer

-   Video content moderation

-   Real-time video processing

When working with videos, it is important to consider how the [videos are
processed into tokens](/docs/tokens#video), which affects
billing and usage limits. You can learn more about prompting with video files in
the [Prompting
guide](/docs/files#prompt-guide).

### Long form audio  {% id="long-form-audio" %}

The Gemini models were the first natively multimodal large language models
that could understand audio. Historically, the typical developer workflow would
involve stringing together multiple domain specific models, like a
speech-to-text model and a text-to-text model, in order to process audio. This
led to additional latency required by performing multiple round-trip requests
and decreased performance usually attributed to disconnected architectures of
the multiple model setup.

Some emerging and standard use cases for audio context include:

- Real-time transcription and translation
- Podcast / video question and answering
- Meeting transcription and summarization
- Voice assistants

The primary optimization when working with long context and the Gemini
models is to use [context
caching](/docs/caching). Beyond the previous
impossibility of processing lots of tokens in a single request, the other main
constraint was the cost. If you have a "chat with your data" app where a user
uploads 10 PDFs, a video, and some work documents, you would historically have
to work with a more complex retrieval augmented generation (RAG) tool /
framework in order to process these requests and pay a significant amount for
tokens moved into the context window. Now, you can cache the files the user
uploads and pay to store them on a per hour basis. The input / output cost per
request with Gemini Flash for example is ~4x less than the standard
input / output cost, so if

In various sections of this guide, we talked about how Gemini models achieve
high performance across various needle-in-a-haystack retrieval evals. These
tests consider the most basic setup, where you have a single needle you are
looking for. In cases where you might have multiple "needles" or specific pieces
of information you are looking for, the model does not perform with the same
accuracy. Performance can vary to a wide degree depending on the context. This
is important to consider as there is an inherent tradeoff between getting the
right information retrieved and cost. You can get ~99% on a single query, but
you have to pay the input token cost every time you send that query. So for 100
pieces of information to be retrieved, if you needed 99% performance, you would

likely need to send 100 requests. This is a good example of where context
caching can significantly reduce the cost associated with using Gemini models
while keeping the performance high.

## FAQs  {% id="faqs" %}

### Where is the best place to put my query in the context window?  {% id="where-is-the-best-place-to-put-my-query-in-the-context-window" %}

In most cases, especially if the total context is long, the model's
performance will be better if you put your query / question at the end of the
prompt (after all the other context).

### Do I lose model performance when I add more tokens to a query?  {% id="do-i-lose-model-performance-when-i-add-more-tokens-to-a-query" %}

Generally, if you don't need tokens to be passed to the model, it is best to
avoid passing them. However, if you have a large chunk of tokens with some
information and want to ask questions about that information, the model is
highly capable of extracting that information (up to 99% accuracy in many
cases).

### How can I lower my cost with long-context queries?  {% id="how-can-i-lower-my-cost-with-long-context-queries" %}

If you have a similar set of tokens / context that you want to re-use many
times, [context caching](/docs/caching) can help reduce the costs
associated with asking questions about that information.

### Does the context length affect the model latency?  {% id="does-the-context-length-affect-the-model-latency" %}

There is some fixed amount of latency in any given request, regardless of the
size, but generally longer queries will have higher latency (time to first
token).

# Long decode

By default, Gemini 4 models (`gemini-4-carbon`, `gemini-4-argon`, and `gemini-4-hydrogen`) generate up to 64K tokens (65,536) of thinking and output per response. Long decode lets you raise `max_output_tokens` past 64K for hard reasoning, math, and coding tasks, up to the unified 1M-token context window (1,048,576 tokens shared across input, thinking, and output). On the Interactions API, you can run long decode with [background execution](/docs/background-execution) so our servers run every hop for you, or in the foreground with [client-side continuation](/docs/long-decode#client-side-continuation).

1. The request runs asynchronously and returns an interaction with `status="in_progress"`.
2. If the response reaches 64K tokens without finishing, the server starts a continuation hop with the tokens generated so far.
3. This repeats until the model finishes or reaches `max_output_tokens`.
4. When you poll the interaction, you get the combined thinking and output from all hops in a single interaction.

To run continuation hops from your client instead, see [Choose how to run long decode](/docs/long-decode#choose-how-to-run-long-decode).

{% tabs %}
  {% tab label="Python" %}
  ```python
  import time
  from google import genai

client = genai.Client()

# 2. Poll until the status is no longer in_progress or queued.
  #    The REST response has no output_text field, so join the text of every model_output step.
  while true; do
    RESP=$(curl -s "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions/$ID" \
      -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY")
    STATUS=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.status')
    if [[ "$STATUS" != "in_progress" && "$STATUS" != "queued" ]]; then
      echo "$RESP" | jq -r '[.steps[]? | select(.type == "model_output") | .content[]? | select(.type == "text") | .text] | join("")'
      echo "$RESP" | jq '{status, usage}'
      break
    fi
    sleep 5
  done
  ```

{% /tab %}

## Output limits  {% id="output-limits" %}

Streaming and non-streaming interactions default to a 64K output token limit, so responses up to 64K tokens need no code changes. To generate past 64K tokens, raise `max_output_tokens` and use background execution or client-side continuation.

| How you create the interaction | Output limit |
| :--- | :--- |
| `background: false`, `max_output_tokens` not set | 65,536 tokens |
| `background: false`, `max_output_tokens` greater than 65,536, `automatic_continuation: true` (SDK default) | Your `max_output_tokens`, up to 1,048,576 minus your input |
| `background: false`, `max_output_tokens` greater than 65,536, `automatic_continuation: false` or REST | 65,536 tokens per streaming hop (or non-streaming hop on `gemini-4-hydrogen`), or 32,768 per non-streaming hop on `gemini-4-carbon` and `gemini-4-argon`. Loop with `continuation_token` to generate up to your `max_output_tokens`. |
| `background: true`, `max_output_tokens` not set | 65,536 tokens |

| Workload | Use long decode? | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Hard math, science, research, and formal proofs | Yes | The model can spend more than 64K tokens to explore and check its reasoning. |
| The hardest coding and agentic tasks | Yes | Some tasks need more than 64K tokens of thinking and code in one response. Most coding and agentic tasks finish under 64K. |
| Evaluation tools that stop at the output limit | Yes | Long decode prevents cut-off answers when the model spends a whole 64K response on thinking. |
| Chat, Q&A, summarization, classification, and extraction | No | These tasks finish well under 32K tokens. |
| Requests for a fixed length, such as "write a 700,000-word book" | No | The model doesn't follow length targets. |

| Agents that call tools in many short turns | No | Each turn is short. Large outputs on each turn fill the shared context window fast. |
| Prompts near the input limit | No | Output can use only 1,048,576 tokens minus your input. |
| Latency-sensitive requests | No | Long decode can run for several minutes. |

Setting a high `max_output_tokens` gives the model room to think longer on hard problems, but the model still decides how much to write. To control how much reasoning effort the model uses, set [`thinking_level`](/docs/thinking).

## Choose how to run long decode  {% id="choose-how-to-run-long-decode" %}

Background execution is the easiest way to run long decode on the Interactions API. Our servers run every hop, so a dropped client connection won't interrupt generation. Client-side continuation, where the Google GenAI SDK or your own code starts each hop, is also available on the Interactions API for foreground calls, stateless requests, or managing your own retry resilience.

|  | Background execution (Interactions API) | Client-side continuation (Interactions API) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Who starts each hop** | Our servers | The Google GenAI SDK (by default), or your own code |
| **Tokens per request** | Your `max_output_tokens`, in one interaction (up to 64K per internal hop) | 64K per stream (and non-streaming on `gemini-4-hydrogen`); 32K per non-streaming request on `gemini-4-carbon` and `gemini-4-argon` |
| **Run time** | Up to 24 hours | 20 minutes per streaming hop, 10 minutes per non-streaming hop |
| **Storage** | Requires `store: true` | Stored by default (`store: true`), or stateless with `store: false` |

| **Best for** | The easiest way to run long decode | Foreground calls, stateless apps, or finer-grained control over retries, so you can build your own backoff, error handling, and resilience |

If you use the GenerateContent API instead, see [long decode with the GenerateContent API](/docs/long-decode?generate-content=true).

## Client-side continuation  {% id="client-side-continuation" %}

The following sections apply when `background: false` (the default). Your client drives each continuation hop instead of our servers, either automatically with the Google GenAI SDK or with your own loop.

while [[ "$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.status')" == "requires_continuation" ]]; do
    echo "$RESP" | jq -rj '[.steps[]? | select(.type == "model_output") | .content[]? | select(.type == "text") | .text] | join("")'
    PREV_ID=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.id')
    TOKEN=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.continuation_token')
    RESP=$(curl -s -X POST "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions" \
      -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d "{
        \"model\": \"gemini-4-carbon\",
        \"previous_interaction_id\": \"$PREV_ID\",
        \"continuation_token\": \"$TOKEN\",
        \"generation_config\": {\"max_output_tokens\": 262144, \"thinking_level\": \"high\"}
      }")
  done

* **Save the interaction ID:** Read it from the `interaction.created` event.
* **Save every `event_id`:** An `event_id` can arrive on `interaction.status_update` events, not only on text deltas.
* **Reconnect with `last_event_id`:** Call `interactions.get` with `stream: true` and the last `event_id`. The stream continues after that event.
* **Read to the end:** After you reconnect, read the stream to the end before you check the status. The server replays missed events, even after the interaction completes.
* **Set long timeouts:** Set HTTP read timeouts to 15 to 20 minutes per stream.

* **Expect output in 5K-token chunks:** After the first 32K tokens on `gemini-4-carbon` and `gemini-4-argon` (or after 64K tokens on `gemini-4-hydrogen`, starting on the second hop), the stream sends output in chunks of about 5,000 tokens at each checkpoint. Pauses between chunks are normal. The interaction isn't stuck, so keep the connection open.

For foreground streams with the Google GenAI SDK, the SDK chains continuation hops into a single stream:

* **Keep reading across hops:** Each hop is its own interaction and emits `interaction.created` and `interaction.completed` events. Don't reset your stream parser on `interaction.created`, and don't stop on `interaction.completed` while status is `requires_continuation`. Save the final hop's ID if you continue the conversation.
* **Handle mid-hop disconnects:** If a connection drops at a checkpoint before new deltas arrive, the SDK reconnects for you. If the stream already yielded deltas after the latest checkpoint, the SDK raises `ContinuationInterruptedError` to avoid duplicate output.

## Interaction status  {% id="background-status" %}

A background interaction can run for up to 24 hours. Once the status is no longer `in_progress` or `queued`, handle the interaction status using this table:

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `completed` | The model finished. | Join the `model_output` steps in `steps` and read `usage`. To continue the conversation, pass this interaction's `id` as `previous_interaction_id`. |
| `requires_continuation` | A foreground hop reached its single-request cap (64K for streaming and `gemini-4-hydrogen` non-streaming, or 32K for `gemini-4-carbon` and `gemini-4-argon` non-streaming) with token budget left. | The Google GenAI SDK continues this for you by default. In REST, send the next hop with `previous_interaction_id` and `continuation_token`. |
| `requires_action` | The model asked for a tool call. | Run the tool. Then send the result with this interaction's `id`. |

| `incomplete` | The model used all of `max_output_tokens`. Text can be empty if the model was still thinking. | Resume with `previous_interaction_id`, `continuation_token`, and a higher `max_output_tokens`, or send the request again with a higher `max_output_tokens`. |
| `failed` | The server couldn't finish, or the interaction ran longer than 24 hours. | Retry the request. If it fails again, share the interaction `id` with support. |
| `cancelled` | You cancelled the interaction. | Read `usage` to see the billed tokens. |

To stop a running interaction, call `client.interactions.cancel(id=interaction.id)` in Python, `client.interactions.cancel(interaction.id)` in JavaScript, or `POST /v1beta/interactions/{id}/cancel` in REST.

## Set `max_output_tokens` {% id="set-max-output-tokens" %}

`max_output_tokens` sets the combined limit for thinking and output across the interaction. Lowering it doesn't make the model think more concisely, and instead cuts the response off sooner.

| Your workload | Recommended `max_output_tokens` |
| :--- | :--- |
| Existing apps with a limit lower than 32K | Raise to 32,768. Background execution isn't needed. |
| Long coding and agentic tasks | Start at 65,536 (the default). Background execution isn't needed. |
| Complex reasoning, hard math, science, and proofs | Set `background: true` (or use client-side continuation) and start at 262,144, up to 1,048,576 minus your input tokens. |

To use fewer tokens, lower `thinking_level`. Use `high` for the hardest reasoning tasks. Use `medium` (the default) for most coding and agentic work.

## Count tokens  {% id="count-tokens" %}

`interaction.usage` reports the totals across all hops. Read these fields: `total_input_tokens`, `total_cached_tokens`, `total_output_tokens`, `total_thought_tokens`, and `total_tokens`.

`total_input_tokens` adds up the input tokens of every hop. Each hop sends your prompt plus everything generated so far back to the model as input, so the same tokens are counted again in every later hop. For example, a 1,000-token prompt that produces 200,000 tokens of thinking and output takes four 64K hops (or seven 32K non-streaming hops on `gemini-4-carbon` and `gemini-4-argon`):

| Hop | Input sent to the model | Input tokens |
| :--- | :--- | ---: |
| 1 | Prompt | 1,000 |
| 2 | Prompt + hop 1 | 66,536 |
| 3 | Prompt + hops 1 and 2 | 132,072 |
| 4 | Prompt + hops 1 to 3 | 197,608 |
| **Total** |  | **397,216** |

`total_input_tokens` reports about 397,000 tokens (with repeated hop inputs automatically discounted 95% by implicit caching), even though the actual context size is only about 201,000 tokens: the 1,000-token prompt plus 200,000 tokens of thinking and output.

## Understand billing  {% id="understand-billing" %}

You pay for every token in every hop, including hops that contain only thinking.

* **Cache discount:** Implicit caching discounts the repeated input in each hop by 95%. Cached input costs $0.10 per 1M tokens instead of $2.00 during the introductory period.
* **Cancelled and failed interactions:** You pay for all work completed before the interaction ends.
## Troubleshooting  {% id="troubleshooting" %}

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
| :--- | :--- |
| Output stops at 64K | Set `max_output_tokens` greater than 65,536, and use background execution or upgrade the Google GenAI SDK. |
| Output stops with status `requires_continuation` | The hop reached its single-request cap with budget left. Upgrade the SDK, enable `automatic_continuation`, or add a continuation loop. |
| 400: "store=true is required for background interactions" | Background execution needs `store: true`. |
| Status `incomplete` with empty text | The model used all tokens on thinking. Raise `max_output_tokens` or lower `thinking_level`. |
| Context compaction starts too early | Your agent framework or evaluation tool reads `total_input_tokens`. See [Count tokens](/docs/long-decode#count-tokens). |

## Limitations  {% id="limitations" %}

* **Earlier SDKs:** Versions earlier than Python 2.34.0, JavaScript 2.32.0, Go 1.77.0, Java 1.80.0, and .NET 1.28.0 don't continue foreground interactions.
* **No length targets:** The model doesn't follow token-length or word-count targets.

# Agents overview

Managed agents on the Gemini API give you a configurable agent
harness. A single API call provisions a Linux sandbox where the agent reasons,
executes code, manages files, and browses the web autonomously.

{% card-grid %}
  {% card description="Make your first agent call, stream responses, and build a custom\nagent." href="/docs/managed-agents-quickstart" icon="rocket_launch" title="Quickstart" /%}

*   **[Deep Research](/docs/deep-research)**: Autonomous research agent
  that plans, executes, and synthesizes multi-step research tasks for use
  cases like market analysis, due diligence, and literature reviews.

## Security and best practices  {% id="security-best-practices" %}

{% callout type="note" %}
  Note: Managed agents are in **Public Preview**. Review the agent's actions and
  outputs before relying on them in sensitive workflows.

{% /callout %}

Every agent runs in a sandboxed environment that is isolated at the OS level.
The sandbox has unrestricted outbound network access by default. You can
restrict or disable network access using an allowlist.

### Network access  {% id="network-access" %}

By default, environments have unrestricted outbound network access. Use a
`network` allowlist to restrict outbound traffic to specific domains or
wildcard patterns. For configuration details, see
[Network Allow List](/docs/aistudio-agents#network-allow-list) (AI
Studio) or [Network rules](/docs/custom-agents#with-network-rules)
(API).

### External tools and APIs  {% id="external-tools-and-apis" %}

You can connect external tools and APIs to extend the agent. Only use tools
from trusted sources and scope permissions to the minimum required. Store
secrets as managed credentials and reference them by ID, so the egress proxy
injects them at request time and they are never exposed inside the sandbox. The agent may use any credential it has access to,
so only provide credentials whose full scope you are willing to grant.

* Use least-privilege service accounts or API keys.
* Prefer short-lived tokens over long-lived keys.
* Only provide credentials whose full scope you are willing to grant.
* Rotate credentials on a regular schedule.

For the credential types and management operations, see
[Credentials](/docs/agent-credentials). You can also set headers inline on an
allowlist rule, see [Network
configuration](/docs/agent-environment#network-configuration).

### Human oversight  {% id="human-oversight" %}

Always verify outputs (generated code, data transformations, configuration
changes) before deploying them, especially for tasks that modify data or
interact with external systems.

## Pricing  {% id="pricing" %}

Managed agents use a [pay-as-you-go model](/docs/pricing#pricing-for-agents) based on Gemini model tokens and tool usage. A single interaction can trigger multiple reasoning loops, typically consuming 100k to 3M tokens. Environment compute is **not billed** during the preview. See [estimated costs](/docs/antigravity-agent#availability-and-pricing) for per-task breakdowns.

## Limits  {% id="limits" %}

| Limit | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Environment Lifetime** | Environments are permanently deleted after 7 days of inactivity. |
| **VM Spin-down** | VMs shut down after a brief period of inactivity to conserve resources. The next request restores the state (with a cold start). |
| **Pre-installed Software** | Ubuntu-based environment with Python 3.12 and Node.js 22. For more information on the environment's base image, see [Pre-installed software](/docs/agent-environment#pre-installed-software). |
| **Max agents** | You can have up to 1,000 managed agents. |

You can also build agents with Gemini using these frameworks and SDKs:

# Managed agents quickstart

This guide walks you through creating and using Managed Agents on the Gemini
API, using the [Antigravity agent](/docs/antigravity-agent). You'll make
your first agent call, continue a multi-turn conversation, stream the response,
download files from the sandbox, and work with the Antigravity managed agent.

## Run your first agent interaction  {% id="run-your-first-agent-interaction" %}

A single call to the [Interactions API](/docs) provisions a Linux sandbox, runs
the agent loop, and returns the result. You'll define three parameters:

* Pass in the `agent` as `"antigravity-preview-09-2026"`, which is the current
  version of our predefined and general purpose managed agent.
* Define `environment="remote"`, to provision a new, fresh sandbox environment.
* Create an input, defining what you want the agent to do.

{% tabs %}
  {% tab label="Python" %}
  ```py
  from google import genai

client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"})

The response returns an `Interaction` object. Store `interaction.id` and
`interaction.environment_id` to continue the conversation in the same sandbox.
Use `interaction.output_text` to access the agent's final response.
`interaction.steps` lists each step the agent took (reasoning, tool calls, code
execution).

## Continue the conversation (multi-turn)  {% id="continue-conversation" %}

The API tracks two independent state dimensions:

- **Conversation context:** chat history, reasoning trace, tool use, using `previous_interaction_id`.
- [**Environment state:**](/docs/agent-environment) files, installed packages and sandbox state, using `environment`.

Pass both in their respective place to resume:

{% tab label="REST" %}
  ```shell
  curl -X POST "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/interactions" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-goog-api-key: $GEMINI_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
      "agent": "antigravity-preview-09-2026",
      "previous_interaction_id": "interaction_id_from_step_1",
      "environment": "environment_id_from_step_1",
      "input": [{"type": "text", "text": "Now plot the Fibonacci sequence as a line chart and save it as chart.png."}]
  }'
  ```

{% /tab %}

{% /tabs %}

Files from turn 1 (`fibonacci.txt`) persist in turn 2. The agent also retains
conversation context.

You can mix and match these independently:

- **Clear conversation, keep files:** Omit `previous_interaction_id`, only pass the environment ID using `environment` for a fresh conversation in the same workspace.
- **Keep conversation, new workspace:** Pass `previous_interaction_id`, set `environment="remote"` for a fresh sandbox.

### Automatic context compaction  {% id="automatic-context-compaction" %}

In long-running, multi-turn conversations, the raw history of reasoning steps,
tool calls, and large file contents can quickly grow and consume significant
context space. To prevent token limit errors and maintain the agent's focus
(preventing "context rot"), the Managed Agents API features a native context
compaction step at around 135k tokens. This happens automatically.

Streaming returns step deltas with incremental updates. When a step completes,
the `step.stop` event includes accumulated usage stats. Learn more in the
[Streaming guide](/docs/streaming).

## Save a managed agent  {% id="save-managed-agent" %}

In the previous steps, we used the default Antigravity agent and customized it
inline. Once you have iterated on your configuration (instructions, skills,
model selection, and environment), you can save it as a reusable managed agent.
This allows you to invoke it by ID without repeating the configuration.

When you save an agent, notice the architectural symmetry with inline
interactions: you specify `base_agent: "antigravity-preview-09-2026"` and can
pass an `agent_config` with your chosen `model` just as you would on
`interactions.create`. You also define a `base_environment` (either from sources
or by forking an existing environment). The agent will use this environment and
model configuration for every new interaction.

**From sources:** Define sources inline, or from other sources such as GitHub
or Cloud Storage.

Client client = Client.builder().httpOptions(HttpOptions.builder().apiVersion("v1beta").build()).build();

Environment env = Environment.builder()
      .sources(List.of(
          Source.builder()
              .type(SourceType.INLINE)
              .target(".agents/AGENTS.md")
              .content("Always include a chart and a summary table in your reports.")
              .build(),
          Source.builder()
              .type(SourceType.REPOSITORY)
              .source("https://github.com/your-org/skills")
              .target(".agents/skills")
              .build()
      ))
      .build();

# Antigravity agent

The Antigravity agent is a general-purpose managed agent on the Gemini API. A single API call gives you an agent that reasons, executes code, manages files, and browses the web inside your own secure Linux sandbox, hosted by Google.

It is built with Gemini 4 Hydrogen and uses the same harness as the Antigravity IDE. You can configure the underlying Gemini model using `agent_config`. Available through the [Interactions API](/docs/interactions-overview) and [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com).

## Capabilities  {% id="capabilities" %}

Each call can provision a Linux sandbox and starts a tool-use loop. The agent plans, acts, observes results, and repeats until the task is done.

- **Code execution:** Run Bash, Python, and Node.js commands. Install packages, run tests, build apps.
- **File management:** Read, write, edit, search, and list files in the sandbox. Files persist across interactions.
- **Web access:** Google Search and URL fetching for data.
- **Context compaction:** Automatic context compaction (triggered at ~135k tokens) to support long-running, multi-turn sessions without losing context or hitting token limits.

See the [Quickstart](/docs/managed-agents-quickstart) for multi-turn usage and streaming.

## Supported tools  {% id="supported-tools" %}

By default, the agent has access to `code_execution`, `google_search`, and `url_context`. Filesystem tools are enabled automatically when you specify the `environment` parameter. You can also define **custom functions** to connect the agent to your own APIs and tools. You only need to specify the `tools` parameter when customizing or restricting the default set, or when adding custom functions.

| Tool | Type value | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Code Execution | `code_execution` | Run shell commands (bash, Python, Node) with stdout/stderr capture. |
| Google Search | `google_search` | Search the public web. |
| URL Context | `url_context` | Fetch and read web pages. |
| Filesystem | *(enabled via `environment`)* | Read, write, edit, search, and list files in the sandbox. The system enables these tools automatically when you set the `environment`. |
| Custom Functions | `function` | Define custom functions that the agent can request to execute. See [Function calling](/docs/antigravity-agent#function-calling). |
| Remote MCP Server | `mcp_server` | Register external Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as tools. See [MCP servers](/docs/antigravity-agent#mcp-servers). |

You can intercept and validate `code_execution` and `filesystem` tool execution right inside the remote sandbox using synchronous [Hooks](/docs/agent-hooks).

To limit the agent to specific tools, pass only the ones you need:

{% tabs %}
  {% tab filename="sample.py" label="Python" %}

interaction = client.interactions.create(
      agent="antigravity-preview-09-2026",
      input="Search for the latest AI research papers on reasoning and summarize them.",
      environment="remote",
      tools=[
          {"type": "google_search"},
          {"type": "url_context"},
      ],
  )

print(interaction.output_text)
  ```

| `url` | string | Yes | The endpoint URL of the remote MCP server. |
| `headers` | object | No | Custom headers (e.g., authentication) sent with requests. |
| `allowed_tools` | array | No | List of tool names allowed to be executed. If omitted, all tools are allowed. |
